title: Refining Prompts for Better Outputs
summary: Students learn a refinement loop - set the goal, judge the output, name one weakness, make a single targeted change, and re-judge - so they can say exactly why a prompt change improved the result.
objectives: Improve a weak prompt so the output better meets the goal.
Explain which change improved the output and why it worked.

body: You ask an AI to 'write about Al Ain' and get a dull, general paragraph. Was the AI wrong - or was the prompt?
Today you become a prompt engineer who sets a clear goal, judges the output against it, and makes one smart change at a time. Best of all, you will be able to say exactly why your change worked.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can turn a weak prompt into a stronger one that better meets the goal.
I can name the exact change I made and explain why it improved the output.
I can judge an output against the goal instead of just accepting it.

terms.definition: The instruction and context you give an AI to guide its output.
What you want the output to achieve, stated clearly.
A limit you set, such as length, tone, or format.
Unclear or open to more than one meaning.
Goal, judge, name the weakness, change, re-judge - repeated.

sections.heading: Judge before you change
body: You cannot improve an output until you judge it honestly against the [[goal]]. Ask: what is missing, and what is off-target?
Common weaknesses in a prompt are a missing audience, missing format, missing [[constraint]], or an [[ambiguous]] task. Naming the weakness tells you exactly what to fix.

sections.heading: Change one thing, and know why
body: Strong refiners change **one thing at a time** and predict why it should help before they test it. That way, when the output improves, they know which change did it.
Specificity comes from the task, the audience, and the format - never from personal or private information. A precise [[prompt]] is not a personal one.

sections.label: Refining is a loop, not a line
sections.heading: Judge, change one thing, judge again
sections.altText: A loop: judge the output you got, change one thing about the prompt, run it again, then judge whether that change helped.
sections.repeatLabel: not good enough yet — go round again
sections.caption: A prompt is rarely right first time, and that is normal. **Keeping the receipts — which change, what happened — is what turns guessing into refining.**

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: You will take a weak prompt with a clear goal, name one weakness, write a targeted v2, predict its effect, and check against the revealed output.
items: Read the weak prompt and its goal.
Judge the v1 output and name one weakness.
Write a v2 that targets only that weakness.
Predict how the output should change and why.
Compare with the revealed v2 output and log it.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Why is changing one thing at a time smarter than changing many?
How can you make a prompt specific without adding any private information?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the one change that most improved your output and why it worked.
Describe a time a clearer instruction would have helped you get a better result in real life.

worksheet.title: Week 2 - Core - Worksheet | Refining Prompts for Better Outputs

questions.prompt: Goal: persuade Grade 6 students to join the chess club. The prompt was: "Write 4 sentences about the chess club for Grade 6 students." The output was 4 clear sentences saying when and where the club meets, but it did not try to persuade anyone to join. Judging the output against the goal, which weakness should you name before writing v2?

options.text: The prompt never says what the writing should do, so the AI just described the club instead of persuading.
The prompt never says who will read it, so the AI wrote for the wrong audience.
The prompt never sets a length, so the AI did not know how much to write.
The prompt contains too many words, so the AI got confused about the topic.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the audience and the length were already in the prompt, so the missing piece was the task itself: 'persuade' was never asked for.
feedback.incorrect: Re-read the prompt: it already names Grade 6 students and asks for 4 sentences, so the gap is the task - it never tells the AI to persuade.

questions.prompt: Sara wants a better notice from her prompt. Put her actions in the order of the refinement loop taught in this lesson.

items.text: She writes v2, changing only the one weakness she named.
She decides what the notice must achieve and writes that goal down.
She judges the v2 output against the same goal to see if it improved.
She reads the v1 output and compares it with her goal.
She names the one weakness that best explains the gap.

feedback.correct: That is the loop: set the goal, judge, name the weakness, make one change, then re-judge against the same goal.
feedback.incorrect: The goal comes first because you cannot judge an output without one, and the weakness must be named before you know what to change.

questions.prompt: Goal: a science-fair notice that Grade 3 students can read on their own. The prompt was "Write a notice about the science fair." The output was correct but used long words like 'methodology' and 'apparatus'. Which changes to the prompt would target that weakness? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Add: "Use short sentences and words an 8-year-old knows."
Add: "Include the date, time and room of the fair."
Add: "Use a formal tone suitable for the school principal."

feedback.correct: Both changes tell the AI who is reading and how to write for them, which is exactly the weakness you named.
feedback.incorrect: The weakness was the reading level, so only changes about the audience or the words used will fix it - adding details, more length or a formal tone does not.

questions.prompt: A student changes the audience, the length and the format of a prompt all at once, and the new output is much better. She can be sure which of those three changes made it better.

feedback.correct: Right - with three changes at once the improvement could come from any of them, which is why refiners change one thing at a time.
feedback.incorrect: A better output only proves that something helped; changing one thing at a time is what lets you say which change caused it.

questions.prompt: Each output below missed the goal in a different way. Match the problem with the single change to the prompt that targets it.

left.text: The notice used words the Grade 3 class could not read.
The answer filled two pages when a short notice was wanted.
The answer came back as one long paragraph when a list was needed.
The answer was about the wrong school event entirely.

right.text: State the exact event the writing is about.
Name who will be reading it.
Ask for the output as a bulleted list.
Set a limit, such as four sentences.

feedback.correct: Each fix targets one named weakness - audience, constraint, format or an ambiguous task - which is why you can tell what caused the improvement.
feedback.incorrect: Name the weakness first, then pick the change that speaks to it: a reading-level problem needs an audience, and a too-long answer needs a limit.

formative.targets: Grade 5 Advanced: refines prompts to improve output quality and explains why
formative.check: Prompt-refinement log: v1 to v2 with a reasoned justification
formative.successCriteria: Makes a refinement that measurably improves the output and explains the causal reason.
